findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Severe dysphagia disproportionate to Parkinson's disease stage; exclude NMJ disorder

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS, orbicularis oculi, nasalis, abductor digiti minimi

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi (facial nerve): Decrement 22% (1st to 4th stimulus) [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Nasalis: Decrement 19% ABNORMAL
  Abductor digiti minimi (ulnar nerve): Decrement 8% NORMAL

HIGH-RATE RNS (50 Hz):
  Abductor digiti minimi: No increment (0% change) — no pathological facilitation

FINDINGS: Significant decremental response in cranial nerve–innervated muscles. No facilitating response on high-rate RNS. A post-synaptic decremental pattern with cranial predominance.

CONCLUSION: Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission with cranial predominance. No pathological facilitation on high-rate stimulation. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Repetitive nerve stimulation: 22% CMAP decrement orbicularis oculi, 19% decrement nasalis — both above 10% threshold. Abductor digiti minimi 8% decrement (normal). No CMAP increment on 50 Hz high-rate stimulation. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission with cranial predominance

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — EXTENSOR DIGITORUM COMMUNIS

Indication: Confirm NMJ dysfunction

RESULTS:
  MCD: 74 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
  Blocking: 32% of potential pairs

CONCLUSION: Markedly increased jitter and blocking. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

Pulmonary function adequate. NIF -62 cm H2O (reference < -60 cm H2O — meets threshold for adequate respiratory reserve). FVC 82% predicted. No immediate respiratory compromise.

output.summary: Late-onset MG in elderly men with bulbar predominance; dysphagia disproportionate to PD severity is the key diagnostic clue

interactions:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — LEVODOPA AND MG TREATMENT

Query: Interaction between levodopa-carbidopa and pyridostigmine/immunosuppressants in patient with PD + MG

FINDINGS:
  LEVODOPA-CARBIDOPA + PYRIDOSTIGMINE:
  - No direct pharmacokinetic interaction
  - Pyridostigmine (AChE inhibitor) may modestly enhance GI motility — beneficial effect on PD-related constipation
  - Caution: both levodopa and pyridostigmine can cause GI side effects; monitor for nausea, diarrhea

  LEVODOPA + PREDNISONE:
  - Corticosteroids may worsen PD symptoms temporarily (orthostatic hypotension, confusion in elderly)
  - Monitor closely when initiating prednisone in elderly patients with PD

  LEVODOPA + MYCOPHENOLATE MOFETIL:
  - No clinically significant interaction

CONCLUSION: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction identified between levodopa-carbidopa and pyridostigmine. Additive gastrointestinal effects are possible; clinical monitoring recommended. Corticosteroids may affect blood pressure and mood in elderly patients; monitoring as clinically indicated.
warnings: No significant levodopa-carbidopa and pyridostigmine pharmacokinetic interaction identified; monitor for additive gastrointestinal side effects. Corticosteroids may transiently affect motor and cognitive function in elderly Parkinson's disease patients; clinical monitoring recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT prescribe metoclopramide for nausea/dysphagia in this PD patient with MG — worsens parkinsonism; use ondansetron or domperidone with caution.
required_recommendations: CT chest — no recurrence; thymoma screening (here negative)
Single-fiber EMG to disambiguate from ALS bulbar onset
Nutritional support and dysphagia precautions (NG feeds or modified diet) given weight loss
Coordinate with Parkinson team — anticipate medication adjustments

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

differential.key_features: Prior NSCLC 7 years ago; surveillance reassuring but paraneoplastic concern persists — PET-CT if any clinical doubt; anti-VGCC and anti-AChR distinguish.
PD can cause dysphagia and dysarthria but does NOT produce fatigable diurnal pattern or RNS decrement.
Bulbar ALS produces dysphagia and dysarthria but with tongue fasciculations/atrophy and UMN signs; EMG shows neurogenic pattern, not NMJ.
Smoker, prior lung cancer — but here AChR positive and pattern is bulbar-predominant fatigable.
Mechanical dysphagia would not produce fatigable ptosis or dysarthria.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Late-onset bulbar-predominant MG can mimic ALS or PD bulbar progression; SFEMG distinguishes NMJ from motor neuron disease.
Significant weight loss warrants early dietitian and SLT consultation; aspiration risk is high.

findings.description:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: Prior right upper lobe lung cancer; progressive dysphagia; exclude recurrence

TECHNIQUE: Multi-detector CT chest with IV contrast, 1mm slices

FINDINGS:
LUNGS: Right upper lobe post-surgical changes with lobectomy defect. No new right upper lobe mass or consolidation. Bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis and patchy peribronchial ground-glass opacities bilaterally, consistent with recurrent aspiration pneumonitis. No pleural effusion.

MEDIASTINUM: No mediastinal or hilar adenopathy. No anterior mediastinal mass. Thymus region: fatty involution (age-appropriate), no thymic mass.

BONES: No lytic or sclerotic lesions. No vertebral metastasis.

UPPER ABDOMEN: Normal liver, spleen, adrenal glands. No hepatic metastasis.

IMPRESSION:
1. No evidence of lung cancer recurrence or new malignancy.
2. Bilateral aspiration pneumonitis changes — consistent with severe dysphagia.
3. No thymic mass or mediastinal adenopathy.

CONCLUSION: No evidence of malignancy or thoracic mass lesion. Bilateral lower lobe changes are consistent with recurrent aspiration. Clinical correlation recommended.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 74-year-old Japanese man with a history of right upper lobe lung cancer resected 7 years ago (no evidence of recurrence at last follow-up 2 years prior) and Parkinson's disease diagnosed 4 years ago was admitted for progressive dysphagia and 11 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 months. He described initial difficulty swallowing solid foods with bolus sticking in his throat, which progressed over several weeks to difficulty with pureed foods and liquids, causing frequent coughing and near-aspiration episodes. He also noted a muffled, hypophonic quality to his voice and nasal regurgitation of liquids on two occasions.

His Parkinson's disease was reasonably controlled; he still shuffled slightly on gait, had mild bilateral resting hand tremor, and occasional freezing episodes, but had been functionally independent in most ADLs until this dysphagia began. He was taking levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily. He had a fixed mild festinating gait attributed to Parkinson's disease for over 3 years without significant change.

The patient had no diplopia, ptosis, or limb weakness. He denied headache, fever, or night sweats. His family expressed concern about a possible cancer recurrence given the prior lung cancer history. On examination, he was moderately wasted (BMI 20.8, down from 24.2 two years ago). Neurological assessment showed impaired pharyngeal reflex and failure on water-swallowing testing with pooling at the base of the tongue. Limb strength was 5/5 bilaterally. Balance was impaired (Berg Balance Scale 36). MMSE was 26. Mild festinating gait was confirmed.

Chest CT showed bilateral lower lobe atelectasis with bronchiectasis and patchy aspiration changes. Admitting team initially attributed dysphagia to Parkinson's disease-related oropharyngeal dysfunction, but the severity was felt disproportionate to Parkinson's disease stage.
